transcript:
Meeting Header:
Date: 2026-03-04
Time: 09:00 PT / 17:00 UTC
Duration: 45m
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE); Samir Patel (Redwood SE); Aisha Gomez (Redwood Solutions); Maya Chen (AtlasPay Head of ML); Carlos Reyes (AtlasPay Platform Eng); Priya Singh (AtlasPay Security); Ethan Wu (AtlasPay SRE)

Auto-summary (auto): Quick sync on Dedicated sizing results, discussion of autoscaling policy parameters and burst capacity, next steps to run capacity validation and share security docs.

Topics:
- POC progress & recent benchmark results
- Autoscaling policy tuning (scale-up/down, cooldowns)
- Burst planning and reserved buffer
- Security / VPC/KMS questions
- Next steps / action items

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan Lee: All right everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call, we got AtlasPay and Redwood on. I think we have 45 minutes, goal today is to review the last week's Dedicated sizing benchmarks and decide autoscaling policy parameters and burst capacity. Samir, you want to start with results?

[00:18] Samir Patel: Yeah sure. So we ran the three main scenarios against the Dedicated preview cluster: steady-state traffic at 50 concurrent requests, a ramp test up to 400 concurrent over 10 minutes, and a sudden burst of 700 concurrent for a two minute spike. Using rw-serve-xl-v1 quantized to int8 for LLM infer, with an average input length ~450 tokens and output ~120 tokens.

[00:42] Maya Chen: Quick question, when you say concurrent, is that RPS or inflight requests? We measure by inflight usually.

[00:48] Samir Patel: Good call — here concurrent == inflight requests. We matched your trace's concurrency distribution. 95th p95 latency for steady-state was ~320ms per response, p95 for the ramp stayed under 450ms, but during the 700 concurrent spike the p95 jumped to ~1.1s and we observed queueing.

[01:10] Carlos Reyes: That 1.1s is kinda high for us — our SLO is 500ms p95. Is that because of model cold start or because the cluster ran out of capacity?

[01:18] Samir Patel: Mostly capacity and batching queuing interactions. The Dedicated pool scales by nodes; when the spike hit we saw autoscaler start adding nodes but there is a 60-90s scale-up window. During that window the runtime increases batching which can increase tail latency. We also saw some KV cache misses at the start of the burst which added extra decode time.

[01:42] Ethan Wu: Do you have metrics on CPU/GPU utilization during the spike? We want to know how much headroom we need in the steady-state pool.

[01:48] Samir Patel: Yes — GPUs were at ~85% on steady state and hit 98-100% during the spike before new nodes came up. So we typically recommend a reserved burst buffer of about 20% headroom at steady-state or configuring burst pools.

[02:04] Jordan Lee: To be explicit, we recommend two levers: reserved buffer in the steady Dedicated pool (so you commit N+ buffer) and an autoscaling burst pool with faster warm nodes. For the latter we can pre-warm a small number of instances with model loaded (warm standby) — that reduces scale-up time to ~20s but costs extra.

[02:24] Priya Singh: From security POV we need clarity on whether warm nodes keep data in memory longer and how logs are handled. Also SOC2 questions — do warm nodes change audit log behavior?

[02:34] Aisha Gomez: Great question. Warm nodes have the model and KV cache loaded but customer data lifetime in memory is the same lifecycle as for regular nodes. All request logs are sent to your VPC-only logging endpoint if configured; we don't retain PII on Redwood side in Dedicated. We'll attach the security docs that explain logging and KMS integration.

[02:56] Maya Chen: Back to autoscaling policies — can you walk thru recommended values? Cooldown, min/max nodes, queue-length thresholds?

[03:04] Samir Patel: Sure. Based on your trace and the benchmark we recommend: min nodes = 4 (to cover baseline 50 inflight with headroom), max nodes = 40 for your projected peak, scale-up threshold: triggered at 70% GPU util OR queue length > 40 per node, scale-up step: +4 nodes, scale-up cooldown: 30s, scale-down cooldown: 300s (5 minutes) to avoid thrash. For burst pool we recommend having 2 warm nodes always, and a fast-path to add up to +12 warm nodes within 20s using pre-warmed images.

[03:42] Carlos Reyes: That sounds reasonable. What about batching? We saw that increasing batch_size to 64 reduced GPU efficiency due to variable sequence length. Any guidance?

[03:52] Samir Patel: Yes, batching is a tradeoff. For your distribution (wide variance in input lengths) we suggest dynamic batching with per-request timeout of 25ms and a max batch size of 48. Also enable prefix KV caching for common prompts — we saw 15% token reduction which helps latency.

[04:12] Maya Chen: Did you try quantization looser than int8? We want better latency but are wary of quality loss.

[04:18] Samir Patel: We benchmarked int8 and bfloat16. bfloat16 gave 10-15% lower latency but higher GPU memory usage which reduces max batch sizes. Int8 gave best cost/latency tradeoff with minimal quality diffs on your eval prompts — we'll include the eval diffs in the spreadsheet.

[04:36] Jordan Lee: Note — for Dedicated pricing, warm nodes count towards reserved capacity for billing. We'll show two scenarios: committed capacity with 20% buffer vs committed + burst-on-demand.

[04:46] Priya Singh: On KMS keys — can you support customer-managed keys in our HSM? We need key control for PII data.

[04:54] Aisha Gomez: Yes, Dedicated supports customer-managed keys via KMS connectors; for on-prem we also have HSM integrations. We'll attach the KMS integration guide.

[05:02] Maya Chen: Quick question on failover — if a region loses capacity, can requests route to another region and still use the KV cache? We rely heavily on prefix cache for reuse.

[05:12] Samir Patel: Cross-region routing is supported but cache locality is per-region. For strict cache consistency you'd want a multi-region cache sync approach which adds complexity; for most cases we recommend region-local cache and rely on fallback model variants in other regions. We can discuss application-level strategies.

[05:36] Carlos Reyes: For the capacity validation run you mentioned — what's the plan? We want it as realistic as possible using our production trace.

[05:44] Samir Patel: Plan is: you share a sanitized production trace (timestamps + tokens + concurrency), we replay it against your Dedicated preview cluster for 4 hours, capture p50/p95/p99 latencies, GPU utilization, queue lengths, and error rates. We'll run two modes: with warm nodes disabled and with 2 warm nodes enabled to compare. We'll produce a results deck and the raw logs.

[06:06] Ethan Wu: How do we connect the replay to our VPC? We can't send traffic through public endpoints.

[06:12] Jordan Lee: We'll run the replay from a VM in your VPC or via a peered testing agent. For security we'll use mutual TLS and the same IAM principals. We'll share the exact instructions in the sizing spreadsheet.

[06:26] Priya Singh: Also need the audit log schema and retention settings — compliance needs that to sign off.

[06:30] Aisha Gomez: We'll attach the audit log schema and SOC2 attestation PDF.

[06:34] Maya Chen: Sounds good. Any surprises in the benchmark that we should be aware of?

[06:38] Samir Patel: Biggest surprise was KV cache miss penalty during cold bursts; pre-warming common prefixes reduced tail by ~200ms. Also quantization interaction with batching was non-linear — sometimes larger batches slowed tail for long sequences.

[06:54] Carlos Reyes: For our initial Dedicated commit, what would you recommend — min nodes 4 with 20% buffer or commit to 12 nodes and avoid burst?

[07:02] Jordan Lee: If you want conservative cost predictability, commit to 12 nodes initially and run the replay to validate; if you want cost optimization, start with 4 + burst pool and iterate. We can model both scenarios in the spreadsheet.

[07:18] Maya Chen: Ok let's close with explicit next steps and owners.

[07:22] Jordan Lee: Action items: Jordan will send updated Dedicated sizing spreadsheet and pricing by Friday (2026-03-06). Samir will schedule the 4-hour capacity validation once you share the trace. Maya to share sanitized trace by Monday (2026-03-09). Priya to confirm KMS/HSM requirements and SOC2 questions by 2026-03-11. We'll schedule a security deep-dive next week.

[07:44] Maya Chen: Thanks all, this was helpful. Looking forward to the replay numbers.

[07:50] Jordan Lee: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up in Slack and send the docs. End meeting.
